name: Hawking-Moss Instanton
description: A homogeneous scalar field at a positive potential maximum on a Euclidean 4-sphere.
convention: We use $c = \hbar = 1$, keep $G$ explicit, and take $\ell$ as the sphere radius at the barrier maximum, with $V_{\mathrm{top}}$ the potential energy density there and $V_F$ the false vacuum energy density. The Euclidean signature is $(+,+,+,+)$, and a dot denotes a derivative with respect to an affine parameter. The Ricci tensor is $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: At the top of a potential barrier, a scalar field rests in an unstable equilibrium. Stephen Hawking and Ian G. Moss used this configuration in 1982 to describe a transition out of a metastable vacuum whose energy sustains exponential expansion [hawking_moss1982]. Their homogeneous solution holds the field at the barrier top throughout a compact Euclidean 4-sphere [weinberg2007hm].¶The potential energy at the maximum sets the radius of this sphere [weinberg2007hm]. A larger positive energy density means a smaller sphere, with stronger curvature. A continuation to real time produces de Sitter geometry with the scalar field still at the maximum [brown2007hm]. A displacement from the maximum starts the field rolling toward one of its neighbouring minima [weinberg2007hm].¶The false vacuum and the barrier top each have their own Euclidean sphere [weinberg2007hm]. For an energy density $V$, the sphere's Euclidean action is $S_E = -3/(8G^2V)$ in units with $c = \hbar = 1$ [weinberg2007hm]. Their action difference is the positive suppression exponent $B = 3(1/V_F - 1/V_{\mathrm{top}})/(8G^2)$, where $V_F$ is the false vacuum energy density and $V_{\mathrm{top}}$ its value at the barrier maximum [weinberg2007hm]. The leading exponential weight is $e^{-B}$ [weinberg2007hm].¶Adam R. Brown and Erick J. Weinberg derived a thermal description of these transitions in 2007, treating the scalar field inside a de Sitter horizon as a system at the horizon's temperature [brown2007hm]. They worked with potential differences small enough that the geometry could be held fixed. In this approximation, the Hawking-Moss exponent is the energy required to raise the field throughout a horizon volume to the barrier top, divided by the de Sitter temperature [weinberg2007hm, brown2007hm]. The thermal construction specifies the field within that horizon volume, with the state beyond the horizon left free [brown2007hm].¶Along suitable families of thick Coleman-De Luccia bounces, the field values at the two poles approach the same barrier maximum [brown2007hm]. Their homogeneous endpoint is the Hawking-Moss saddle. Brown and Weinberg also identified potentials for which a Coleman-De Luccia bounce coexists with a Hawking-Moss solution carrying one negative fluctuation mode [brown2007hm]. The dominant decay channel depends on the competing actions.¶For a fixed false vacuum, equal potential heights at distant maxima produce equal Hawking-Moss action differences [weinberg2007hm]. Weinberg related these saddle weights to thermal occupation probabilities and showed that a decay calculation must restrict the contributing states to the chosen false vacuum [weinberg2007hm]. Daiki Saito and Naritaka Oshita studied remote transitions in 2025 using a homogeneous scalar field on a fixed de Sitter background, with thermal and stochastic noise switched off [saito2025hm]. For their linear potential and stated regime of validity, the quantum transition probability retains dependence on the field separation, with greater suppression at larger separations [saito2025hm].

related.text: The sphere at the barrier maximum continues to de Sitter space with the same constant scalar field [brown2007hm].
A family of thick vacuum bubbles can approach the homogeneous field at a barrier maximum [brown2007hm]. The two saddles can also coexist for the same potential.
A round Euclidean 4-sphere enters both constructions. The Hawking-Moss exponent compares a whole sphere at the barrier maximum with a false vacuum sphere [weinberg2007hm].

coordinates.name: Euclidean 4-Sphere

parameters.description: The barrier maximum sphere radius, $\ell^2 = 3/(8\pi G V_{\mathrm{top}})$.

coordinates.convention: We use the proper distance $\xi$ from one pole, with $\chi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ angles on each 3-sphere.

coordinates.name: Euclidean Thermal Coordinates

parameters.description: The barrier maximum sphere radius, $\ell^2 = 3/(8\pi G V_{\mathrm{top}})$.

coordinates.convention: We use the Euclidean time $\tau$ of period $2\pi\ell$, the areal radius $r$, and the polar angles $\theta$ and $\phi$.

coordinates.name: Euclidean Thermal Angle

parameters.description: The barrier maximum sphere radius, $\ell^2 = 3/(8\pi G V_{\mathrm{top}})$.

coordinates.convention: We use the Euclidean time $\tau$ of period $2\pi\ell$ and the radial angle $\eta$, where $r = \ell\sin\eta$, with $\theta$ and $\phi$ polar angles.

coordinates.name: Static Constant Field Continuation

parameters.description: The barrier maximum sphere radius, $\ell^2 = 3/(8\pi G V_{\mathrm{top}})$.

coordinates.convention: We continue $\tau = it$ with $t$ a length, and use the areal radius $r$ and the polar angles $\theta$ and $\phi$ in signature $(-,+,+,+)$.

coordinates.name: Wall Constant Field Continuation

parameters.description: The barrier maximum sphere radius, $\ell^2 = 3/(8\pi G V_{\mathrm{top}})$.

coordinates.convention: We continue $\chi = \pi/2 + i\psi$, with $\psi$ a dimensionless time and $\xi$ a length, in signature $(+,-,+,+)$.

coordinates.name: Closed Constant Field Continuation

parameters.description: The barrier maximum sphere radius, $\ell^2 = 3/(8\pi G V_{\mathrm{top}})$.

coordinates.convention: We continue $\xi = \pi\ell/2 + it$, with $t$ a proper time measured as a length and $\chi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ angles, in signature $(-,+,+,+)$.
